Selection Sort.problem: Sort an int array in nondecreasing order in place and return the same array.
Selection Sort.approach: Pick the smallest value from the unsorted suffix and place it at its first position. After pass i, the prefix contains the i+1 smallest values in sorted order.
Selection Sort.complexity: O(n²) comparisons in every case; O(1) auxiliary space. Not stable.
Selection Sort.pitfalls: Empty, singleton, duplicate, sorted and reverse-sorted arrays are valid. Quick sort with Lomuto partition still degenerates on all-equal input; random pivot does not remove that case. Deep recursion can exhaust the stack.
Selection Sort.alternatives: For large general arrays use Arrays.sort in application code. Compare these algorithms by stability, memory, and worst-case behavior rather than only average runtime.

Bubble Sort.problem: Sort an int array in nondecreasing order in place and return the same array.
Bubble Sort.approach: Swap adjacent inversions. Each pass settles the largest remaining value at end. A pass with no swaps proves the array is sorted.
Bubble Sort.complexity: O(n²) worst/average time, O(n) best time; O(1) space. Stable because equal values are never swapped.
Bubble Sort.pitfalls: Empty, singleton, duplicate, sorted and reverse-sorted arrays are valid. Quick sort with Lomuto partition still degenerates on all-equal input; random pivot does not remove that case. Deep recursion can exhaust the stack.
Bubble Sort.alternatives: For large general arrays use Arrays.sort in application code. Compare these algorithms by stability, memory, and worst-case behavior rather than only average runtime.

Insertion Sorting.problem: Sort an int array in nondecreasing order in place and return the same array.
Insertion Sorting.approach: Maintain a sorted prefix. Shift strictly larger values right, then insert the next key into the gap.
Insertion Sorting.complexity: O(n²) worst/average time, O(n) best time; O(1) space. Stable.
Insertion Sorting.trace: [3,1,2]: insert 1 before 3, then insert 2 between 1 and 3.
Insertion Sorting.pitfalls: Empty, singleton, duplicate, sorted and reverse-sorted arrays are valid. Quick sort with Lomuto partition still degenerates on all-equal input; random pivot does not remove that case. Deep recursion can exhaust the stack.
Insertion Sorting.alternatives: For large general arrays use Arrays.sort in application code. Compare these algorithms by stability, memory, and worst-case behavior rather than only average runtime.

Merge Sorting.problem: Sort an int array in nondecreasing order in place and return the same array.
Merge Sorting.approach: Divide the half-open interval [l,r) in two, sort both halves, then merge by repeatedly selecting the smaller front value. Sorted fronts ensure the next selected value is globally smallest among remaining entries.
Merge Sorting.complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) buffer plus O(log n) stack. Stable due to left-first equality.
Merge Sorting.trace: [3,1,2]: sort [3] and [1,2], then merge fronts 3/1, 3/2, leftover 3.
Merge Sorting.pitfalls: Empty, singleton, duplicate, sorted and reverse-sorted arrays are valid. Quick sort with Lomuto partition still degenerates on all-equal input; random pivot does not remove that case. Deep recursion can exhaust the stack.
Merge Sorting.alternatives: For large general arrays use Arrays.sort in application code. Compare these algorithms by stability, memory, and worst-case behavior rather than only average runtime.

Quick Sorting.problem: Sort an int array in nondecreasing order in place and return the same array.
Quick Sorting.approach: Randomly select a pivot and move it to the end. Partition into values smaller than pivot and values at least pivot; place pivot between them, then recurse on both sides.
Quick Sorting.complexity: Expected O(n log n), worst O(n²) time. Expected O(log n), worst O(n) stack. Not stable.
Quick Sorting.trace: With pivot 2 in [3,1,2], move 1 left, place 2 at index 1, then sort the one-element sides.
Quick Sorting.pitfalls: Empty, singleton, duplicate, sorted and reverse-sorted arrays are valid. Quick sort with Lomuto partition still degenerates on all-equal input; random pivot does not remove that case. Deep recursion can exhaust the stack.
Quick Sorting.alternatives: For large general arrays use Arrays.sort in application code. Compare these algorithms by stability, memory, and worst-case behavior rather than only average runtime.

Recursive Bubble Sort.problem: Sort an int array in nondecreasing order in place and return the same array.
Recursive Bubble Sort.approach: One pass settles the maximum at n-1. Recursively sort the remaining prefix; no-swap early termination is valid.
Recursive Bubble Sort.complexity: O(n²) worst time, O(n) best time; O(n) worst stack. Stable.
Recursive Bubble Sort.trace: [3,1,2] bubbles 3 to the end; recurse on [1,2] and stop.
Recursive Bubble Sort.pitfalls: Empty, singleton, duplicate, sorted and reverse-sorted arrays are valid. Quick sort with Lomuto partition still degenerates on all-equal input; random pivot does not remove that case. Deep recursion can exhaust the stack.
Recursive Bubble Sort.alternatives: For large general arrays use Arrays.sort in application code. Compare these algorithms by stability, memory, and worst-case behavior rather than only average runtime.

Recursive Insertion Sort.problem: Sort an int array in nondecreasing order in place and return the same array.
Recursive Insertion Sort.approach: First recursively sort n-1 entries, then insert the last entry into that sorted prefix.
Recursive Insertion Sort.complexity: O(n²) worst time, O(n) best time; O(n) stack even for sorted input. Stable.
Recursive Insertion Sort.trace: Sort [3,1] into [1,3], then insert 2 to obtain [1,2,3].
Recursive Insertion Sort.pitfalls: Empty, singleton, duplicate, sorted and reverse-sorted arrays are valid. Quick sort with Lomuto partition still degenerates on all-equal input; random pivot does not remove that case. Deep recursion can exhaust the stack.
Recursive Insertion Sort.alternatives: For large general arrays use Arrays.sort in application code. Compare these algorithms by stability, memory, and worst-case behavior rather than only average runtime.
